Title: Rome in World Time, Part 12: The Long Goodbye: Manzikert to the Fall of Constantinople (AD 1025–1461)

Summary: The last four centuries of the Roman Empire: palace coups and popular uprisings, defeat at Manzikert, the Crusades, the sack of Constantinople by Crusaders in 1204, exile and recovery, ruinous civil wars, the Ottoman advance, and the final siege of 1453, followed by the fall of the last Roman outposts in 1460–1461. Over the same years the Mongols built the largest land empire in history, the Black Death crossed the world, Mali's Mansa Musa travelled to Mecca, Ming China sent treasure fleets to Africa, and the Hundred Years' War ended in the same summer that Constantinople fell.

---

Basil II left behind the strongest state in the Christian world. Within 50 years it was in serious trouble, and within 200 years its capital had been sacked by the very Crusaders it asked for help. This final post follows the empire to its end, and to its very last pieces, more than 2,200 years after the traditional founding of Rome.

## After Basil (1025–1081): from strength to crisis

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1028–1056 | Basil's niece **Zoe** and her husbands and adopted son rule. The army is neglected; the currency starts to slide |
| 1038–1040 | General **George Maniakes** retakes much of Sicily from the Arabs, then is recalled |
| **1040–1041** | **Peter Delyan** leads a Bulgarian uprising |
| **April 1042** | **Popular revolution in Constantinople**: when Michael V exiles the beloved Empress Zoe, the city rises, storms the palace and blinds him. Zoe and her sister Theodora rule jointly |
| 1043 | **Maniakes** revolts in Italy and marches on Constantinople, but dies in battle. A Rus fleet attacks the capital |
| 1047 | **Leo Tornikios** revolts and besieges the capital |
| **16 Jul 1054** | **East–West Schism**: papal legates excommunicate the Patriarch of Constantinople, who excommunicates them back |
| 1057 | The generals' revolt makes **Isaac I Komnenos** emperor |
| April 1071 | The Normans take **Bari**, the last Roman city in Italy |
| **26 Aug 1071** | **Manzikert**: the Seljuk sultan **Alp Arslan** defeats and captures **Romanos IV**. Civil war follows, and Turkish groups flood into Anatolia |
| 1078 | Revolts of Nikephoros Bryennios and Nikephoros Botaneiates |

## The Komnenoi and the Crusades (1081–1185)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1081 | **Alexios I Komnenos** seizes the throne. Normans under Robert Guiscard invade the Balkans and win at **Dyrrhachium** |
| 1082 (or 1092) | Alexios gives **Venice** huge trading privileges for naval help; the Venetians become powerful in the empire |
| 1091 | With Cuman help, Alexios annihilates the Pechenegs at Levounion |
| 1095 | Alexios asks the Pope for western soldiers; Urban II preaches the **First Crusade** at Clermont |
| 1097 | Crusaders and Romans take **Nicaea** |
| 1099 | The Crusaders take **Jerusalem** and keep it and Antioch for themselves, against their oaths to Alexios |
| 1118–1143 | **John II Komnenos**, considered the best of the dynasty |
| 1143–1180 | **Manuel I Komnenos**, a pro-western emperor; Second Crusade passes through (1147) |
| **12 Mar 1171** | Manuel arrests every Venetian in the empire and seizes their goods |
| 1176 | **Myriokephalon**: Manuel's army is ambushed by the Seljuks; he compares it to Manzikert |
| **1182** | **Massacre of the Latins**: a mob in Constantinople kills thousands of Italian residents |
| 1183–1185 | **Andronikos I** seizes power through terror |
| 1185 | The Normans sack **Thessalonica**. A mob tears Andronikos to pieces in the Hippodrome |
| **1185–1186** | The brothers **Asen and Peter** lead a revolt in Bulgaria; the Second Bulgarian Empire is born |
| 1185–1191 | A rebel Komnenos rules **Cyprus** until Richard the Lionheart takes it on his way to the Third Crusade |

## 1204: the sack of Constantinople

The **Fourth Crusade** was supposed to attack Egypt. It owed Venice money for its fleet, and it agreed to put the exiled prince **Alexios IV** on the throne in return for payment. When the money never came and Alexios IV was murdered in a palace coup, the Crusaders stormed the city.

On **13 April 1204** the Crusaders broke in and sacked Constantinople for three days. Churches were looted, Hagia Sophia was stripped, and the bronze horses that now stand at St Mark's in Venice were carried off. The empire was divided:

| Successor state | Who | What happened to it |
|---|---|---|
| **Latin Empire** | Crusaders at Constantinople | Weak from the start; its first emperor Baldwin was captured by the Bulgarians at Adrianople in 1205 |
| **Empire of Nicaea** | Theodore Laskaris, in western Anatolia | The strongest Roman successor; retook Constantinople in 1261 |
| **Despotate of Epirus** | A branch of the Angelos family, in western Greece | A rival claimant until the 1230 defeat at Klokotnitsa |
| **Empire of Trebizond** | The Grand Komnenoi, on the Black Sea | Founded weeks before the sack, with Georgian help; lasted until 1461 |
| Venice | Islands and ports | Took Crete and key harbours |

## Restoration and decline (1261–1402)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1222–1254 | **John III Vatatzes** makes Nicaea prosperous and strong |
| **25 Jul 1261** | Nicaean troops find a gate open and **retake Constantinople**. **Michael VIII Palaiologos** is crowned |
| 1274 | Michael VIII agrees to church union with Rome at the Council of Lyon to stop Charles of Anjou's planned invasion; his own people revolt against the union |
| 1282 | The **Sicilian Vespers** revolt destroys Charles of Anjou's plans (Michael VIII helped fund it) |
| **1302** | **Bapheus**: **Osman**, founder of the Ottomans, beats a Roman army near Nicomedia |
| **1303–1311** | The **Catalan Company**, hired mercenaries, turn on the empire after their leader Roger de Flor is murdered (1305) and pillage Thrace and Greece |
| 1321–1328 | Civil war between **Andronikos II** and his grandson **Andronikos III** |
| 1326 | The Ottomans take **Bursa** |
| 1331, 1337 | Nicaea and Nicomedia fall to the Ottomans |
| **1341–1347** | Civil war between **John Kantakouzenos** and the regency for John V; both sides hire Turks and Serbs |
| **1342–1350** | The **Zealots** take over Thessalonica in a popular revolution against the aristocracy |
| 1346 | **Stefan Dušan** of Serbia crowns himself emperor |
| **1347** | The **Black Death** reaches Constantinople from Caffa |
| 1354 | An earthquake ruins Gallipoli's walls; the Ottomans occupy it, their first base in Europe |
| c. 1369 (disputed) | The Ottomans take **Adrianople** and later make it their capital |
| 1371 | Serbian defeat at the Maritsa river; the emperor becomes an Ottoman vassal |
| **1373** | **Andronikos IV** and the Ottoman prince **Savcı** jointly revolt against their fathers; it fails |
| 1376–1379 | Andronikos IV usurps the throne with Genoese and Ottoman support |
| 1389 | **Kosovo**: the Serbs and Ottomans fight; both leaders die |
| 1394–1402 | Sultan **Bayezid I** blockades Constantinople |
| 1396 | **Nicopolis**: a Crusade to relieve the empire is destroyed |
| 1399–1403 | Emperor **Manuel II** tours Europe seeking help; he spends Christmas 1400 in England with Henry IV |
| **1402** | **Ankara**: **Timur** (Tamerlane) crushes and captures Bayezid. The siege is lifted; Constantinople gets 50 more years |

## The end (1402–1461)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1422 | Murad II besieges Constantinople and fails |
| 1430 | **Thessalonica** falls to the Ottomans after eight years under Venetian control |
| 1438–1439 | **Council of Ferrara–Florence**: John VIII agrees to church union for western help. Most of his people reject it |
| 1444 | **Varna**: a Crusade is destroyed; the Polish-Hungarian king dies |
| 1449 | **Constantine XI Palaiologos** becomes the last emperor |
| 1452 | **Mehmed II** builds the Rumeli Hisarı fortress on the Bosporus |
| 6 Apr 1453 | The siege begins. Mehmed has about 60,000–80,000 men and the huge cannon of the Hungarian engineer **Orban**. The defenders number about 7,000, including Genoese under **Giovanni Giustiniani** |
| 22 Apr 1453 | The Ottomans drag ships overland into the Golden Horn |
| **29 May 1453** | The final assault. Giustiniani is wounded and withdraws; the Ottomans break in. **Constantine XI** dies fighting, his body never certainly identified. Mehmed rides to Hagia Sophia and makes it a mosque |
| 1460 | The Despotate of the **Morea** (at Mystras) falls |
| **15 Aug 1461** | **Trebizond** surrenders. The last Roman state with an emperor ends |
| 1475 | The small Greek principality of **Theodoro** in Crimea, the last fragment, falls |

### What happened to the idea of Rome

- **Mehmed II** took the title *Kayser-i Rum*, Caesar of Rome.
- **Moscow** married Ivan III to Constantine XI's niece Sophia Palaiologina (1472) and later called itself the "Third Rome." Russian rulers took the title *tsar*, from Caesar.
- The **Holy Roman Empire** in the West, descended from Charlemagne's title, lasted until **1806**.
- Greek scholars who fled to Italy helped fuel the **Renaissance**.

## Things you might not have known happened at the same time

**Constantinople fell in the same summer the Hundred Years' War ended.** Castillon, on 17 July 1453, was won partly by French cannon. Seven weeks earlier Ottoman cannon had broken the walls of Constantinople. Gunpowder ended both the medieval castle and the ancient city wall in the same season.

**Two emperors captured, 1449 and 1402.** In 1449 the Mongols captured the Ming emperor at Tumu, the same year Constantine XI was crowned. In 1402 Timur captured the Ottoman sultan Bayezid at Ankara, which saved Constantinople for half a century.

**Baghdad fell to the Mongols just before Constantinople was retaken.** The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate. Three years later the Romans retook Constantinople. The Mongols' destruction of the Seljuks (1243) also helped Nicaea survive.

**The Crab Nebula was "born" in the year of the Schism.** In July 1054, Chinese astronomers recorded a new star bright enough to see in daylight. That same month, the churches of Rome and Constantinople excommunicated each other.

**The printing press and the fall of Constantinople were contemporary.** Gutenberg was perfecting his press as Mehmed planned his siege. Greek refugees and their manuscripts reached Italy just as the technology to copy them cheaply arrived.

## Closing the series: Rome's whole story in one table

| Era | Years | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Kingdom (trad.) | 753–509 BC | ~244 years |
| Republic | 509–27 BC | ~482 years |
| Principate (united empire) | 27 BC–AD 284 | ~311 years |
| Late empire (united, then split) | 284–476/480 | ~195 years |
| Eastern Roman ("Byzantine") Empire alone | 476–1453 | ~977 years |
| Last fragments (Morea, Trebizond, Theodoro) | to 1461/1475 | |
| **Total, founding to 1453** | | **about 2,206 years** |

For context: in 753 BC the Assyrians ruled Mesopotamia and the Zhou ruled China. In 1453 the Ming ruled China, the Inca were building Machu Picchu, and Columbus was a toddler in Genoa. Rome, in one form or another, was there for all of it.

## Sources and notes

- Michael Psellos, *Chronographia* (976–1078), an insider's view of the palace revolutions.
- Michael Attaleiates, *History* (an eyewitness of Manzikert).
- Anna Komnene, *The Alexiad*, the history of her father Alexios I, one of the first histories written by a woman.
- Niketas Choniates, *Annals* (to 1206, an eyewitness of 1204).
- Geoffrey of Villehardouin and Robert of Clari, Crusader accounts of the Fourth Crusade.
- John Kantakouzenos, *Histories*, and Nikephoros Gregoras, *Roman History* (the 14th-century civil wars).
- Doukas, George Sphrantzes, Laonikos Chalkokondyles and Kritoboulos of Imbros, for 1453 from both sides; Nicolò Barbaro's diary of the siege.
- Steven Runciman, *The Fall of Constantinople 1453* (1965); Jonathan Harris, *The End of Byzantium* (2010); Anthony Kaldellis, *The New Roman Empire* (2023).
- Overview: [Battle of Manzikert (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Manzikert), [Sack of Constantinople (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Constantinople), [Fall of Constantinople (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople), [Empire of Trebizond (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Trebizond).

**Flags:** The date of Alexios I's privileges to Venice (1082 or 1092) is debated. The date the Ottomans took Adrianople ranges from 1361 to 1369 in different studies. Troop numbers for the 1453 siege vary widely between sources; the figures given here are common modern estimates. The founding dates of Mali (c. 1235) and Tenochtitlan (c. 1325) and Pachacuti's accession (c. 1438) are traditional. Black Death mortality estimates vary by region. The "total years" figure uses the traditional, legendary founding date of 753 BC.
